claim: SATB1 forms a nuclear substructure that resists high-salt extraction.
source: SATB1 forms a nuclear substructure that resists high-salt extraction.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known property of SATB1.

claim: SATB1 binds base-unpairing regions (BURs), genomic elements with high unwinding propensities.
source: SATB1 binds base-unpairing regions (BURs), genomic elements with high unwinding propensities.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is a central finding of the study.

claim: In mouse thymocytes, SATB1 establishes a two-tiered chromatin organization: one through indirect binding to transcriptionally active DNase 1-accessible chromatin and another by direct binding to BURs in the DNase 1-inaccessible nuclear substructure.
source: In mouse thymocytes, we found that SATB1 establishes a two-tiered chromatin organization: one through indirect binding to transcriptionally active DNase 1-accessible chromatin and another by direct binding to BURs in the DNase 1-inaccessible nuclear substructure.
evidence: This is a major finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data from urea ChIP-seq and standard ChIP-seq.

claim: Recently published ChIP-seq datasets show SATB1 binding to accessible chromatin at enhancers and CTCF sites, but not to BURs.
source: Recently published ChIP-seq datasets show SATB1 binding to accessible chromatin at enhancers and CTCF sites, but not to BURs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and refers to prior published work using standard ChIP-seq methods.

claim: By employing urea ChIP-seq, which retains only directly bound protein:DNA complexes, BURs, but not CTCF sites, are direct SATB1 binding targets genome-wide.
source: By employing urea ChIP-seq, which retains only directly bound protein:DNA complexes, we found that BURs, but not CTCF sites, are direct SATB1 binding targets genome-wide.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study, supported by urea ChIP-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BURs bound to the SATB1 nuclear substructure interact with accessible chromatin, crossing multiple topologically associated domains (TADs).
source: BURs bound to the SATB1 nuclear substructure interact with accessible chromatin, crossing multiple topologically associated domains (TADs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by urea 4C-seq data showing long-range interactions.

claim: SATB1 is required for megabase-scale interactions linked to cell-type-specific gene expression.
source: SATB1 is required for these megabase-scale interactions linked to cell-type-specific gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by urea 4C-seq data comparing wild-type and SATB1-knockout cells.

claim: BURs are highly enriched within transcriptionally repressive lamina-associated domains (LADs).
source: BURs are highly enriched within transcriptionally repressive lamina-associated domains (LADs).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genome-wide analysis comparing BUR distribution with LAD maps.

claim: SATB1 anchors some BURs (18%) outside LADs near genes in otherwise accessible chromatin to the SATB1 nuclear substructure.
source: Besides these BURs, SATB1 anchors some BURs (18%) outside LADs near genes in otherwise accessible chromatin to the SATB1 nuclear substructure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by quantitative analysis of SATB1-bound BURs in LADs versus inter-LADs.

claim: Only a subset of total BURs is bound to SATB1, depending on cell type.
source: Only a subset of total BURs is bound to SATB1, depending on cell type.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by urea ChIP-seq data from different cell types (thymocytes, brain, skin).

claim: Despite the mutually exclusive SATB1-binding profiles uncovered by the two ChIP-seq methods, most peaks in both profiles are valid and require SATB1.
source: Notably, despite the mutually exclusive SATB1-binding profiles uncovered by the two ChIP-seq methods, we found most peaks in both profiles are valid and require SATB1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq experiments in SATB1-knockout cells showing loss of peaks.

claim: The SATB1 protein network forms a chromatin scaffold, providing an interface that connects accessible chromatin to a subnuclear architectural structure, thereby facilitating the three-dimensional organization linked to cell-type-specific gene expression.
source: Based on these and previous data, we propose that the SATB1 protein network forms a chromatin scaffold, providing an interface that connects accessible chromatin to a subnuclear architectural structure, thereby facilitating the three-dimensional organization linked to cell-type-specific gene expression.
evidence: This is the main model proposed in the abstract, based on the integration of current findings with previous data.

claim: Three-dimensional (3D) chromatin architecture, formed by chromatin folding at multiple hierarchical levels, is thought to play a fundamental role in genome activity such as gene expression.
source: Three-dimensional (3D) chromatin architecture, formed by chromatin folding at multiple hierarchical levels, is thought to play a fundamental role in genome activity such as gene expression (Politz et al., 2013; van Steensel and Belmont, 2017; Schoenfelder and Fraser, 2019; Bashkirova and Lomvardas, 2019; Göndör and Ohlsson, 2018; Loubiere et al., 2020; Misteli, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: High-resolution chromatin interaction maps have revealed chromatin to be partitioned mainly into two types of megabase (Mb)-sized compartments, A and B.
source: High-resolution chromatin interaction maps, generated by chromosome conformation capture methods such as Hi-C (all-to-all contacts), have revealed chromatin to be partitioned mainly into two types of megabase (Mb)-sized compartments, A and B (Lieberman-Aiden et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to the Lieberman-Aiden et al. 2009 study.

claim: The euchromatic A compartment is gene-rich, transcriptionally active, and enriched in histone marks associated with active chromatin, conferring high chromatin accessibility.
source: The euchromatic A compartment is gene-rich, transcriptionally active, and enriched in histone marks associated with active chromatin, conferring high chromatin accessibility.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about chromatin compartments.

claim: The B compartment is gene-poor, transcriptionally repressive, and enriched in repressive histone marks.
source: On the other hand, the B compartment is gene-poor, transcriptionally repressive, and enriched in repressive histone marks.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about chromatin compartments.

claim: The largely transcriptionally repressive lamina-associated domains (LADs) are among the B compartment chromatin displaying the typical features of heterochromatin.
source: The largely transcriptionally repressive lamina-associated domains (LADs) are among the B compartment chromatin displaying the typical features of heterochromatin (Guelen et al., 2008; Kind et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: LADs have been identified by the lamin B1-mediated adenine methyltransferase identification (DamID) method as genomic regions that are spatially proximal to the nuclear lamina.
source: LADs have been identified by the lamin B1-mediated adenine methyltransferase identification (DamID) method (van Steensel et al., 2001) as genomic regions that are spatially proximal to the nuclear lamina, an intermediate filament meshwork adjacent to the inner nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to the van Steensel et al. 2001 study.

claim: LADs represent discrete chromatin domains of 10 kb to 10 Mb in size in mouse and human cells.
source: LADs represent discrete chromatin domains of 10 kb to 10 Mb in size in mouse and human cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about LAD sizes.

claim: Approximately 1000–1500 LADs have been identified in mouse and human cells and they cover greater than 30% of the genome.
source: Approximately 1000–1500 LADs have been identified in these cells and they cover greater than 30% of the genome (Guelen et al., 2008; Peric-Hupkes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Chromatin domains called 'topological-associated domains' (TADs) were detected that are relatively insulated from adjacent TADs by preferentially making intra-domain contacts via looping.
source: At sub-megabase scales, using Hi-C, chromatin domains called 'topological-associated domains' (TADs) were previously detected that are relatively insulated from adjacent TADs by preferentially making intra-domain contacts via looping (Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012; Sexton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CTCF and cohesin are the two major architectural proteins required for folding chromatin into loops.
source: CTCF and cohesin are the two major architectural proteins required for folding chromatin into loops.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge.

claim: The loop extrusion model postulates that cohesin functions in loop extrusion until it encounters the CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) bound to its target sites in a convergent orientation.
source: The loop extrusion model postulates that cohesin functions in loop extrusion until it encounters the CCCTC-binding factor (CTCF) bound to its target sites in a convergent orientation (Sanborn et al., 2015; Fudenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: CTCF- and cohesin-binding sites are enriched at the boundaries of TADs and LADs.
source: CTCF- and cohesin-binding sites are enriched at the boundaries of TADs (Dixon et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2014) and LADs (Guelen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Acute depletion of CTCF, cohesin or induced removal of cohesin loading factor NIPBL results in a major loss of TADs.
source: Acute depletion of CTCF (Nora et al., 2017), cohesin (Rao et al., 2017; Wutz et al., 2017) or induced removal of cohesin loading factor NIPBL (Schwarzer et al., 2017) results in a major loss of TADs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The majority of protein-coding genes remained largely unchanged in their expression levels in the absence of TADs.
source: Unexpectedly, the majority of protein-coding genes remained largely unchanged in their expression levels in the absence of TADs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from prior studies on CTCF/cohesin depletion.

claim: Super-resolution live-cell imaging studies revealed that chromatin looping formed by CTCF and cohesin is highly dynamic and variable among individual single cells.
source: In the last few years, using super-resolution live-cell imaging, genome interactions were studied at the single cell levels. These studies revealed that chromatin looping formed by CTCF and cohesin is highly dynamic and variable among individual single cells, suggesting that TADs are an emergent property of the cell population average of heterogeneous chromatin folding (Cattoni et al., 2017; Bintu et al., 2018; Finn et al., 2019; Gabriele et al., 2022; Mach et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: SATB1 was originally identified by virtue of its specific binding to genomic sequences called Base Unpairing Regions (BURs).
source: SATB1 was originally identified by virtue of its specific binding to genomic sequences called Base Unpairing Regions (BURs).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as historical background on SATB1.

claim: Previous in vitro studies have shown that SATB1 directly binds BURs without requiring additional molecules, such as RNA or proteins.
source: Previous in vitro studies have shown that SATB1 directly binds BURs without requiring additional molecules, such as RNA or proteins (Kohwi-Shigematsu and Kohwi, 1990; Bode et al., 1992; Dickinson et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: BURs have a strong unwinding property under negative superhelical stress.
source: BURs have a strong unwinding property under negative superhelical stress, and BURs are empirically identified using unpaired DNA-specific chemical probes (Kohwi-Shigematsu and Kohwi, 1990; Kohwi-Shigematsu and Kohwi, 1992) because they lack primary sequence consensus.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A typical BUR (~200–300 bp) contains a cluster of short sequence segments (25–50 bp/segment) containing exclusively As, Ts, and Cs on one strand (ATC context).
source: However, BURs have a unique sequence context: a typical BUR (~200–300 bp) contains a cluster of short sequence segments (25–50 bp/segment) containing exclusively As, Ts, and Cs on one strand (ATC context; Kohwi-Shigematsu and Kohwi, 1990; Dickinson et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: BURs are at least 65% AT-rich, but not all AT-rich sequences are BURs.
source: BURs are at least 65% AT-rich, but importantly, not all AT-rich sequences are BURs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a defining characteristic of BURs.

claim: SATB1 binds to BURs in the minor groove of double-stranded DNA, recognizing the altered phosphate backbone structure; it does not bind to single-stranded DNA.
source: Importantly, SATB1 binds to BURs in the minor groove of double-stranded DNA, recognizing the altered phosphate backbone structure; it does not bind to single-stranded DNA (Dickinson et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Disruption of the ATC context by mutagenesis, without affecting the AT content, results in loss of unwinding property of a BUR and SATB1 binding.
source: Disruption of the ATC context by mutagenesis, without affecting the AT content, results in loss of unwinding property of a BUR and SATB1 binding.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as evidence for the importance of ATC context.

claim: SATB1 protein is cell-type restricted, most abundantly expressed in thymocytes and among multiple immature progenitor cells of adult tissues, as well as terminal differentiated postnatal neurons in the cortex and amygdala.
source: While BURs are obviously present in the genome across cell types, SATB1 protein is cell-type restricted, most abundantly expressed in thymocytes and among multiple immature progenitor cells of adult tissues (Fessing et al., 2011; Alvarez et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2019), as well as terminal differentiated postnatal neurons in the cortex and amygdala (Balamotis et al., 2012; Huang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: SATB1 has an interconnected cage-like distribution in thymocytes and a fine spider web-like distribution in neurons forming a unique SATB1-rich subnuclear architecture that is resistant to high-salt extraction.
source: Located in the nuclear interior, SATB1 has an interconnected cage-like distribution in thymocytes (Cai et al., 2003) and a fine spider web-like distribution in neurons (Balamotis et al., 2012) forming a unique SATB1-rich subnuclear architecture that is resistant to high-salt extraction.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Some BURs have been identified and characterized as in vivo SATB1 binding sites and, when bound to SATB1, are also resistant to salt extraction.
source: Some BURs have been identified and characterized as in vivo SATB1 binding sites and, when bound to SATB1, are also resistant to salt extraction (Cai et al., 2003; de Belle et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: SATB1 has been shown to be essential for loop formation connecting a subset of BURs and recruiting chromatin remodeling complexes, epigenetic factors, and transcription factors to specific gene loci.
source: SATB1 has been shown to be essential for loop formation connecting a subset of these BURs and recruiting chromatin remodeling complexes, epigenetic factors, and transcription factors to specific gene loci (Kohwi-Shigematsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to prior review.

claim: SATB1 regulates expression of hundreds of protein-coding genes in a cell-type-specific manner to enable cells to acquire new phenotypes.
source: Of particular interest, SATB1 regulates expression of hundreds of protein-coding genes in a cell-type-specific manner to enable cells to acquire new phenotypes, such as during T cell activation (Cai et al., 2006), development of many adult progenitor cells (Fessing et al., 2011; Balamotis et al., 2012; Alvarez et al., 2000; Zhang et al., 2019, Skowronska-Krawczyk et al., 2014; Hao et al., 2015; Kakugawa et al., 2017; Kitagawa et al., 2017; Yasuda et al., 2019; Goolam and Zernicka-Goetz, 2017; Satoh et al., 2013), and cancer metastasis (Kohwi-Shigematsu et al., 2013; Han et al., 2008; Ordinario et al., 2012; Frömberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: SATB1 plays an essential role in the development of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, NKT cells, and Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Treg) in the thymus.
source: For example, by directing lineage-specific transcriptional programs, SATB1 plays an essential role in the development of CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, NKT cells, and Foxp3+ regulatory T cells (Treg) in the thymus (Kakugawa et al., 2017; Kitagawa et al., 2017) as well as in promoting the pathogenic effector program of tissue Th17 cells in autoimmune disease in mice (Yasuda et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: SATB1 mediates co-induction of interleukin genes in T helper cells and regulates ~1000 genes in cancer to promote metastasis.
source: These activities have been shown to mediate co-induction of interleukin genes in T helper cells (Cai et al., 2006) and regulate ~1000 genes in cancer to promote metastasis (Han et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The genome-wide SATB1 binding profiles obtained by the widely used, standard chromatin immunoprecipitation-deep sequencing (ChIP-seq) do not detect SATB1 interaction with BURs.
source: Although BURs have been identified to be specific and direct binding target sequences of SATB1, mysteriously, the genome-wide SATB1 binding profiles obtained by the widely used, standard chromatin immunoprecipitation-deep sequencing (ChIP-seq) do not detect SATB1 interaction with BURs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key observation motivating the current study.

claim: SATB1 has been mapped mainly to enhancers and to a region that would become an active super-enhancer upon differentiation by standard ChIP-seq.
source: Instead, SATB1 has been mapped mainly to enhancers and to a region that would become an active super-enhancer upon differentiation (Hao et al., 2015; Kakugawa et al., 2017; Kitagawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Recent studies on chromatin looping with Hi-C show that SATB1 mediates interactions involving a subset of enhancers and promoters for cell identity gene expression and that SATB1 binding sites coincide with many CTCF-bound loci.
source: In line with this, recent studies on chromatin looping with Hi-C also show that SATB1 mediates interactions involving a subset of enhancers and promoters for cell identity gene expression and that SATB1 binding sites coincide with many CTCF-bound loci (Feng et al., 2022; Zelenka et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Standard ChIP-seq approaches have several drawbacks including biased capture of transcriptionally active, highly accessible 'open' chromatin and generation of false-positive 'phantom' peaks.
source: ChIP-seq has been a gold standard for profiling chromatin-protein interactions. However, standard ChIP-seq approaches have several drawbacks. First, chromatin structure can introduce biases into ChIP-seq analysis. Fragmentation of crosslinked chromatin in whole cells/nuclei can result in biased capture of transcriptionally active, highly accessible 'open' chromatin and generation of false-positive 'phantom' peaks (Jain et al., 2015; Park et al., 2013; Teytelman et al., 2013; Meyer and Liu, 2014; Baumgarten and Bryant, 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Standard ChIP-seq fails to distinguish between direct and indirect (piggybacking) chromatin binding of a protein of interest.
source: Second, it fails to distinguish between direct and indirect (piggybacking) chromatin binding of a protein of interest.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of standard ChIP-seq.

claim: Urea ChIP-seq first isolates stringently purified whole intact genomic DNA that retains only its directly bound proteins from crosslinked cells prior to fragmentation and immunoprecipitation.
source: Here, we optimized urea-ChIP-seq, a modified ChIP-seq that first isolates stringently purified whole intact genomic DNA that retains only its directly bound proteins from crosslinked cells prior to fragmentation and immunoprecipitation.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the urea ChIP-seq method.

claim: Urea ChIP-seq captures the entire genome, regardless of its original chromatin accessibility status.
source: This captures the entire genome, regardless of its original chromatin accessibility status.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of urea ChIP-seq.

claim: Urea ChIP-seq allowed identification of genomic sites directly bound by SATB1 and revealed BURs to be the primary direct SATB1 target sites, previously hidden by standard ChIP-seq.
source: This approach has allowed us to identify genomic sites directly bound by SATB1 and revealed BURs to be the primary direct SATB1 target sites, previously hidden by standard ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: The SATB1-bound BURs are mutually exclusive with enhancer-enriched SATB1-bound sites mapped by standard ChIP-seq.
source: The SATB1-bound BURs are mutually exclusive with enhancer-enriched SATB1-bound sites mapped by standard ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: A majority of BURs are mapped within LADs.
source: Instead, a majority of BURs are mapped within LADs, and depending on cell type, SATB1 binds in vivo to selective subsets of these BURs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: Depending on cell type, SATB1 binds in vivo to selective subsets of BURs.
source: Instead, a majority of BURs are mapped within LADs, and depending on cell type, SATB1 binds in vivo to selective subsets of these BURs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: Select SATB1-bound BURs were found to interact extensively over the >5.7 Mb gene-rich region within DNase 1 hypersensitive (DNase 1 HS) regions, but not with adjacent gene-poor regions.
source: Using the urea 4C-seq (one-to-all contacts), select SATB1-bound BURs were found to interact extensively over the >5.7 Mb gene-rich region within DNase 1 hypersensitive (DNase 1 HS) regions, but not with adjacent gene-poor regions.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: SATB1 is essential for both megabase-level chromatin interactions and proper expression of multiple genes in the gene-rich region.
source: SATB1 is essential for both megabase-level chromatin interactions and proper expression of multiple genes in this gene-rich region.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: SATB1-mediated genome organization exhibits two distinct features: a 'skeletal framework' where SATB1 binds BURs directly, and a network of gene-rich open chromatin that is tethered to BURs indirectly through SATB1-mediated chromatin looping, which is correlated to gene expression.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that SATB1-mediated genome organization exhibits two distinct features, a 'skeletal framework' where SATB1 binds BURs directly, and a network of gene-rich open chromatin that is tethered to BURs indirectly through SATB1-mediated chromatin looping, which is correlated to gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: After extraction of nuclei with buffer containing 2 M NaCl that removed most of the proteins from DNA, individually cloned SATB1-bound BURs remained anchored to the residual SATB1 protein network (SATB1-rich subnuclear architecture) found in the interior of nuclei.
source: Consistent with this, after extraction of nuclei with buffer containing 2 M NaCl that removed most of the proteins from DNA, individually cloned SATB1-bound BURs remained anchored to the residual SATB1 protein network (SATB1-rich subnuclear architecture) found in the interior of nuclei (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: In high-salt extracted Satb1-/- (SATB1-KO) thymocyte nuclei, BURs lost their anchored sites and were exclusively found in the distended DNA halos that spread around the residual nuclei.
source: By contrast, in high-salt extracted Satb1-/- (SATB1-KO) thymocyte nuclei, these BURs lost their anchored sites and were exclusively found in the distended DNA halos that spread around the residual nuclei, which is illustrated (Figure 1A) (Cai et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Without prior formaldehyde crosslinking, urea centrifugation removes 99.9% of chromatin-associated protein from chromatin and sediments unsheared pure genomic DNA at the bottom of the tube.
source: It is important to note that without prior formaldehyde crosslinking, urea centrifugation removes 99.9% of chromatin-associated protein from chromatin and sediments unsheared pure genomic DNA at the bottom of the tube (Kohwi-Shigematsu et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: High concentrations of urea (e.g. 6–8 M) disrupt the secondary structures of nucleic acids and the three-dimensional structure of proteins.
source: As a denaturant for DNA, RNA, and proteins, high concentrations of urea (e.g. 6–8 M) disrupt the secondary structures of nucleic acids and the three-dimensional structure of proteins (Das and Mukhopadhyay, 2009; Raghunathan et al., 2020; Oprzeska-Zingrebe and Smiatek, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Purified genomic DNA obtained from 8 M urea ultracentrifugation remains double-stranded and can be readily digested with restriction enzymes.
source: Crucially, purified genomic DNA obtained from 8 M urea ultracentrifugation remains double-stranded and can therefore be readily digested with restriction enzymes this study and (Kohwi-Shigematsu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study and current data.

claim: The proteins that remain bound to urea-purified DNA from crosslinked cells can still be detected with the antibodies compatible with standard ChIP protocols.
source: Additionally, the proteins that remain bound to urea-purified DNA from crosslinked cells can still be detected with the antibodies compatible with standard ChIP protocols.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a property of urea-purified chromatin.

claim: High concentrations of urea destabilize double-stranded DNA by weakening the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, thereby decreasing the melting temperature of DNA.
source: By acting as both a hydrogen bond donor and acceptor, high concentrations of urea destabilize double-stranded DNA by weakening the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, thereby decreasing the melting temperature of DNA (Kourilsky et al., 1970; Kourilsky et al., 1971).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Even 6–8 M urea alone, without heat treatment, is insufficient to convert double-stranded DNA into single-stranded DNA.
source: However, even 6–8 M urea alone, without heat treatment, is insufficient to convert double-stranded DNA into single-stranded DNA (Hegedüs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The 8 M urea centrifugation protocol lacks heat treatment and includes prior formaldehyde fixation, thus allowing genomic DNA to remain double-stranded and bound by interacting proteins.
source: Our 8 M urea centrifugation protocol lacks heat treatment and includes prior formaldehyde fixation, thus allowing genomic DNA to remain double-stranded and bound by interacting proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a key feature of the urea ChIP-seq method.

claim: The urea ChIP-seq method allows detection of genomic regions solely based on their direct protein binding regardless of their original chromatin status, such as 'accessible' or 'inaccessible' chromatin.
source: Critically, the urea ChIP-seq method (Kohwi-Shigematsu et al., 2012) allows detection of genomic regions solely based on their direct protein binding regardless of their original chromatin status, such as 'accessible' or 'inaccessible' chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a key advantage of urea ChIP-seq.

claim: Urea ChIP-seq produced SATB1 binding profiles that are entirely different from those produced by the standard ChIP-seq method.
source: Strikingly, urea ChIP-seq produced SATB1 binding profiles that are entirely different from those produced by the standard ChIP-seq method (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only 0.92% (an average of two replicates per ChIP-seq method) of peaks in urea SATB1 ChIP-seq coincided with those in standard SATB1 ChIP-seq.
source: The genome-wide analysis in mouse thymocytes using deepTools revealed that only 0.92% (an average of two replicates per ChIP-seq method) of peaks in urea SATB1 ChIP-seq coincided with those in standard SATB1 ChIP-seq (Supplementary files 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative analysis.

claim: In a large genomic region covering a 4.48 Mb region in chromosome 17, a gene-rich region was found in the valley between BUR-enriched domains, and standard ChIP-seq detects clusters of SATB1 binding sites in this gene-rich region.
source: In a large genomic region covering a 4.48 Mb region in chromosome 17 (Figure 2A), a gene-rich region was found in the valley between BUR-enriched domains (Figure 2A, track 3), and standard ChIP-seq detects clusters of SATB1 binding sites in this gene-rich region (Figure 2A, tracks 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Urea ChIP-seq detected SATB1-binding to the domains surrounding the gene rich region, corresponding to regions heavily enriched in BUR sites.
source: In contrast, urea ChIP-seq detected SATB-binding to the domains surrounding the gene rich region, corresponding to regions heavily enriched in BUR sites (Figure 2A, tracks 3–5).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: SATB1 sites identified from urea ChIP-seq precisely coincided with BUR peaks and are excluded in the standard SATB1 ChIP-seq peaks.
source: In a zoomed-in view, covering a 430 kb region that includes a gene-rich region, SATB1 sites identified from urea ChIP-seq precisely coincided with BUR peaks and are excluded in the standard SATB1 ChIP-seq peaks (Figure 2B, tracks 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SATB1 bound sites uncovered from urea ChIP-seq avoided CTCF sites, H3K27ac-marked sites and DNase 1 hypersensitive (HS) regions.
source: SATB1 bound sites uncovered from urea ChIP-seq avoided CTCF sites (Figure 2B, tracks 4 and 5 versus track 6), H3K27ac-marked sites and DNase 1 hypersensitive (HS) regions (Figure 2B tracks 7 and 8), whereas SATB1 sites from standard ChIP-seq primarily co-mapped to these sites (Figure 2B, tracks 1,2,6–9).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Among SATB1 urea ChIP-seq peaks, an average of 77% of two replicates coincided with BURs identified in the reference maps.
source: Among SATB1 urea ChIP-seq peaks, an average of 77% of two replicates coincided with BURs identified in our reference maps (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The statistical significance of enrichment of BURs compared to a random overlap in urea ChIP-seq peaks is p<0.001.
source: The statistical significance of enrichment of BURs compared to a random overlap in either urea ChIP-seq or standard ChIP-seq peaks is p<0.001 or p=1, respectively, using 1000 bootstrapped genomic intervals sampled using the bootRanges approach (Mu et al., 2023) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The statistical significance of enrichment of BURs compared to a random overlap in standard ChIP-seq peaks is p=1.
source: The statistical significance of enrichment of BURs compared to a random overlap in either urea ChIP-seq or standard ChIP-seq peaks is p<0.001 or p=1, respectively, using 1000 bootstrapped genomic intervals sampled using the bootRanges approach (Mu et al., 2023) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: While SATB1 binding profiles by standard ChIP-seq specifically exclude BURs, showing a sharp indentation at the peak of BUR distribution, SATB1-binding profiles by urea ChIP-seq coincide with BUR distribution.
source: Consistent with this, genome-wide distribution profile analyses show that while SATB1 binding profiles by standard ChIP-seq specifically exclude BURs, showing a sharp indentation at the peak of BUR distribution, SATB1-binding profiles by urea ChIP-seq coincide with BUR distribution (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SATB1 predominantly and directly tethers BURs genome-wide in vivo to the DNase 1-inaccessible nuclear substructure which is depleted in CTCF and enhancers.
source: These results indicate that SATB1 predominantly and directly tethers BURs genome-wide in vivo to the DNase 1-inaccessible nuclear substructure which is depleted in CTCF and enhancers.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the urea ChIP-seq data.

claim: The SATB1-binding profiles obtained by standard and urea ChIP-seq methods are mutually exclusive.
source: In other words, the SATB1-binding profiles obtained by standard and urea ChIP-seq methods are mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a key observation.

claim: Urea ChIP-seq, which solely captures DNA with its directly bound proteins, unmasks SATB1 direct binding profiles missed by standard ChIP-seq.
source: We conclude that our urea ChIP-seq, which solely captures DNA with its directly bound proteins, unmasks SATB1 direct binding profiles missed by standard ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the comparison of the two methods.

claim: The DNA-binding profile for CTCF by urea ChIP-seq was very similar to that obtained by standard ChIP-seq from ENCODE, which largely overlapped with DNase 1 HS peaks.
source: We investigated the DNA-binding profile for CTCF by urea ChIP-seq and found its profile to be very similar to that obtained by standard ChIP-seq from ENCODE, which largely overlapped with DNase 1 HS peaks (Davis et al., 2018) (Figure 3A, tracks 2, 4, 5, and 6).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Urea ChIP-seq generated essentially identical DNA-binding profiles for polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) core subunits, SUZ12, JARID2, and EZH2 as generated by others using standard ChIP-seq.
source: Similarly, we also found that urea ChIP-seq generated essentially identical DNA-binding profiles for polycomb repressive complex 2 (PRC2) core subunits, SUZ12, JARID2, and EZH2 as generated by others using standard ChIP-seq (Peng et al., 2009) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 37% of SATB1 peaks from standard ChIP-seq (ENCODE) (average of two replicates) intersected with CTCF peaks genome-wide.
source: In line with recent studies (Feng et al., 2022; Zelenka et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023), 37% of SATB1 peaks from standard ChIP-seq (ENCODE) (average of two replicates, Supplementary file 1) intersected with CTCF peaks genome-wide.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative analysis.

claim: Only 0.8% of SATB1 peaks from urea ChIP-seq coincided with CTCF peaks (average of two replicas).
source: In contrast, only 0.8% of SATB1 peaks from urea ChIP-seq coincided with CTCF peaks (average of two replicas, Supplementary file 1), confirming the UCSC browser track views (Figures 2A and 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative analysis.

claim: Urea ChIP-seq can accurately identify the DNA-binding sites of chromatin-associated proteins.
source: These results verify that urea ChIP-seq can accurately identify the DNA-binding sites of chromatin-associated proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the CTCF and PRC2 data.

claim: Urea ChIP-seq, compared to standard ChIP-seq, produces contrasting DNA-binding profiles for SATB1, but this is not necessarily the case for other nuclear proteins.
source: Thus, urea ChIP-seq, compared to standard ChIP-seq, produces contrasting DNA-binding profiles for SATB1, but this is not necessarily the case for other nuclear proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from comparing SATB1 with CTCF and PRC2.

claim: Only urea ChIP-seq can faithfully detect direct and specific SATB1 interactions with BURs, suggesting a different mode of chromatin interactions.
source: Importantly, only urea ChIP-seq can faithfully detect direct and specific SATB1 interactions with BURs, suggesting a different mode of chromatin interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the comparison of the two methods.

claim: CTCF-binding profiles mapped by urea ChIP-seq showed no major changes depending on SATB1.
source: We validated this result by generating the CTCF-binding profiles by urea ChIP-seq in Satb1-/- (SATB1-KO) and Satb1+/+ (SATB1-WT) thymocytes. These CTCF-binding profiles showed no major changes depending on SATB1 (Figure 3A, compare tracks 2 and 3), as shown in a randomly chosen region in chromosome 17 in wild-type (WT) and SATB1-KO thymocytes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: CTCF urea ChIP-seq peak distributions from SATB1-WT and SATB1-KO thymocytes coincided genome-wide.
source: This was confirmed by genome-wide analyses which showed that CTCF urea ChIP-seq peak distributions from SATB1-WT and SATB1-KO thymocytes coincided (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CTCF binding to genomic DNA is SATB1-independent genome-wide.
source: This indicates that CTCF binding to genomic DNA is SATB1-independent genome-wide.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the CTCF urea ChIP-seq data in WT and KO cells.

claim: SATB1-bound urea-ChIP fragments contained SATB1 as expected, but neither CTCF nor RAD21 (a cohesin complex component) was detected in the SATB1 urea-ChIP samples.
source: Urea-purified crosslinked-chromatin fragments immunoprecipitated with anti-SATB1 antibody (SATB1-bound urea-ChIP fragments) contained SATB1 as expected, detected by western blot of the de-crosslinked urea-ChIP sample. However, neither CTCF nor RAD21 (a cohesin complex component) was detected in the SATB1 urea-ChIP samples.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by urea ChIP-Western data.

claim: Reciprocal experiments using either CTCF or RAD21-bound urea ChIP samples confirmed lack of SATB1 co-binding to these chromatin fragments.
source: Reciprocal experiments using either CTCF or RAD21-bound urea ChIP samples confirmed lack of SATB1 co-binding to these chromatin fragments (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Figure 3—source data 1, Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C and supplements.

claim: At least for the direct DNA co-binding status of SATB1 with either CTCF or RAD21, SATB1 does not co-bind chromatin with either of these proteins.
source: Therefore, these results from urea ChIP-Western indicate that at least for the direct DNA co-binding status of SATB1 with either CTCF or RAD21, SATB1 does not co-bind chromatin with either of these proteins (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fragments co-bound by RAD21 and CTCF represent only a small fraction of either total RAD21-bound or CTCF-bound chromatin fragments.
source: As expected, we do find co-binding; however, fragments co-bound by RAD21 and CTCF represent only a small fraction of either total RAD21-bound or CTCF-bound chromatin fragments (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CTCF and RAD21 direct co-binding to chromatin occurs much less frequently than their individual binding to chromatin.
source: These results show that CTCF and RAD21 direct co-binding to chromatin occurs much less frequently than their individual binding to chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the urea ChIP-Western data.

claim: Bulk Hi-C results revealed largely indistinguishable TAD profiles between wild-type (Satb1+/+:Cd4-Cre) and SATB1-deficient (Satb1fl/fl:Cd4-Cre) thymocytes examined at 10 kb resolution.
source: We compared bulk Hi-C results between thymocytes isolated from wild-type (Satb1+/+:Cd4-Cre) and SATB1-deficient (Satb1fl/fl:Cd4-Cre) mice in duplicates (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B). Our Hi-C results revealed largely indistinguishable TAD profiles between the two thymocytes (Figure 3D) examined at 10 kb resolution.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Hi-C data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Neither TAD number nor TAD sizes were changed by SATB1 depletion from thymocytes.
source: Neither TAD number nor TAD sizes were changed by SATB1 depletion from thymocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Intra-TAD interactivity (the sum of Hi-C chromatin contacts inside the TAD) also remained mostly unchanged upon SATB1 deletion.
source: Intra-TAD interactivity (the sum of Hi-C chromatin contacts inside the TAD) also remained mostly unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D.

claim: SATB1 depletion did not alter segregation of active (A) and inactive chromatin compartmentalization (B).
source: Similar to the results from the CTCF depletion study (Nora et al., 2017), SATB1 depletion also did not alter segregation of active (A) and inactive chromatin compartmentalization (B) (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3E and supplement.

claim: SATB1 depletion does not affect chromosome compaction.
source: Furthermore, our scaling plot displaying how the Hi-C contacts decrease as a function of genomic distance shows that SATB1 depletion does not affect chromosome compaction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: SATB1 and CTCF are two independent proteins that have distinct roles in chromatin organization, consistent with SATB1 having no roles in TAD organization.
source: These Hi-C re,sults taken together with SATB1-independent CTCF-binding to DNA and non-overlapping direct genomic DNA-binding of SATB1 and CTCF/cohesin, strongly suggest that SATB1 and CTCF are two independent proteins that have distinct roles in chromatin organization, consistent with SATB1 having no roles in TAD organization.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the Hi-C and ChIP data.

claim: Both antibodies (1583 and ab109112) generated similar peaks in KO thymocytes (KO peaks) by standard ChIP-seq.
source: To address this question, we performed standard ChIP-seq on Satb1-/- (KO) thymocytes using two different anti-SATB1 antibodies (1583 and ab109112, both of which are validated for immunoprecipitation). The results are highlighted in two randomly chosen ~3 Mb regions in chromosome 17 and in the X chromosome, each containing a gene-rich region surrounded by gene-poor regions. Both antibodies generated similar peaks in KO thymocytes (KO peaks) by standard ChIP-seq.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the validation experiment.

claim: KO peaks (false positives) were predominantly detected in gene-rich, open chromatin regions in KO thymocytes, and many of them coincided with peaks originally detected in WT thymocytes.
source: These KO peaks (false positives) were predominantly detected in gene-rich, open chromatin regions in KO thymocytes, and many of them coincided with peaks originally detected in WT thymocytes (WT peaks; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B, top and bottom, tracks 9 and 10).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: 4.1% of SATB1 standard ChIP-seq peaks obtained from our experiments are false-positive peaks (based on average of two standard KO ChIP-seq samples).
source: Intersection analyses with deepTools show that 4.1% of SATB1 standard ChIP-seq peaks obtained from our experiments are false-positive peaks (based on average of two standard KO ChIP-seq samples; Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative analysis.

claim: SATB1 urea ChIP-seq had no false-positive peaks (0.0%).
source: In contrast, SATB1 urea ChIP-seq had no false-positive peaks (0.0%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative analysis.

claim: Only ~100 KO-specific peaks (not overlapping with WT peaks) were detected (average of two samples) compared to ~40,000 total WT peaks from SATB1 urea ChIP-seq.
source: Also, only ~100 KO-specific peaks (not overlapping with WT peaks) were detected (average of two samples) compared to ~40,000 total WT peaks from SATB1 urea ChIP-seq (Supplementary files 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative analysis.

claim: Most SATB1 sites detected from standard ChIP-seq are bound by SATB1, but most likely through indirect binding, as these peaks are not detected by urea ChIP-seq.
source: After validation with SATB1-KO cells, we conclude that most SATB1 sites detected from standard ChIP-seq are bound by SATB1, but most likely through indirect binding, as these peaks are not detected by urea ChIP-seq, which removes any indirect binding proteins by urea ultracentrifugation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the validation experiments.

claim: By either direct urea-ChIP or standard ChIP, SATB1-bound sites within all three loci (Rag1/2, Foxp3, and Runx3) were found to be SATB1-dependent.
source: By either direct urea-ChIP or standard ChIP, we found SATB1-bound sites within all three loci (Rag1/2, Foxp3, and Runx3) to be SATB1-dependent. These sites were detected only in WT (Figure 4, track 3) but not in SATB1 KO-thymocytes (Figure 4, tracks 7 and 9 for Rag/Rag2 and Runx3, and tracks 9 and 11 for Foxp3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: SATB1 has been shown by standard ChIP-seq to bind the anti-silencer element (ASE) at the Rag1 and Rag2 loci and this binding is thought to counteract the activity of an intergenic silencer, thus promoting expression of Rag 1 and Rag 2.
source: For the Rag1 and Rag2 loci, SATB1 has been shown by standard ChIP-seq to bind the anti-silencer element (ASE) and this binding is thought to counteract the activity of an intergenic silencer, thus promoting expression of Rag 1 and Rag 2 (Hao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: During the development of Foxp3+-regulatory T cells (Treg) in the thymus, SATB1 expression in Treg precursor cells is essential for the future establishment of a Treg cell–specific super-enhancers at the Foxp3 locus in Treg cells.
source: During the development of Foxp3+-regulatory T cells (Treg) in the thymus, SATB1 expression in Treg precursor cells is essential for the future establishment of a Treg cell–specific super-enhancers at the Foxp3 locus in Treg cells (Kitagawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Thymocyte precursor-specific SATB1 deficiency, using Satb1fl/fl:Cd4-Cre mice but not Satb1fl/fl:Foxp3-Cre mice, impairs Treg super-enhancer activation and expression of Foxp3.
source: Thus, thymocyte precursor-specific SATB1 deficiency, using Satb1fl/fl:Cd4-Cre mice but not Satb1fl/fl:Foxp3-Cre mice, impairs Treg super-enhancer activation and expression of Foxp3 (Kitagawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: SATB1 is essential for the generation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and NKT cells.
source: Finally, SATB1 is also essential for the generation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells and NKT cells (Kakugawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: In response to T cell receptor signaling by MHC class I and II, SATB1 regulates enhancer function in gene loci encoding lineage-specifying factors (e.g. Runx3) and directs lineage-specific transcriptional programs in the thymus.
source: In response to T cell receptor signaling by MHC class I and II, SATB1 regulates enhancer function in gene loci encoding lineage-specifying factors (e.g. Runx3) and directs lineage-specific transcriptional programs in the thymus (Kakugawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: In the three regions (Rag1/Rag2, Foxp3, and Runx3), SATB1-bound BURs, as detected by urea ChIP-seq, are found infrequently and appear as isolated single peaks within 30–50 kb regions.
source: Strikingly, in these three regions, SATB1-bound BURs, as detected by urea ChIP-seq, are found infrequently and appear as isolated single peaks within 30–50 kb regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the observation at these loci.

claim: SATB1-bound BUR sites reside within 3 kb of the nearest putative SATB1-bound enhancers (detected by standard ChIP-seq) for the Rag1/Rag2 and Runx3 loci as well as from the super-enhancer that becomes established at the Foxp3 loci in matured Treg cells.
source: Such SATB1-bound BUR sites are located close to but not overlapping with the cluster of enhancers marked by H3K27ac and H3Kme1 modifications. These SATB1-bound BUR sites reside within 3 kb of the nearest putative SATB1-bound enhancers (detected by standard ChIP-seq) for the Rag1/Rag2 and Runx3 loci as well as from the super-enhancer that becomes established at the Foxp3 loci in matured Treg cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the spatial relationship between BURs and enhancers.

claim: While the SATB1-bound peaks generated by urea ChIP and standard ChIP-seq did not overlap, they were nonetheless proximal to each other, and both were SATB1 dependent.
source: Results from these three loci show that, while the SATB1-bound peaks generated by urea ChIP and standard ChIP-seq did not overlap, they were nonetheless proximal to each other, and both were SATB1 dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the analysis of the three loci.

claim: The two distinct ChIP-seq protocols are likely detecting two different modes of DNA binding for SATB1 that is direct binding to BURs and indirect binding to open chromatin regions.
source: The two distinct ChIP-seq protocols are likely detecting two different modes of DNA binding for SATB1 that is direct binding to BURs and indirect binding to open chromatin regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the comparison of the two methods.

claim: BUR-1 interacts extensively over a 5.8 Mb gene-rich region in wild-type thymocytes.
source: In wild-type thymocytes, we detected BUR-1 making extensive long-distance interactions covering most of the ~5.8 Mb adjacent gene-rich region (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by urea 4C-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: BUR-1 interactions are found to be scarce over the gene-desert region upstream of BUR-1, despite the presence of many SATB1-bound BURs in this region.
source: Interestingly, BUR-1 interactions are found to be scarce over the gene-desert region upstream of BUR-1, despite the presence of many SATB1-bound BURs in this region (Figure 5A, top track for urea SATB1 ChIP-seq, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A and supplement.

claim: BUR-1 interactions were found particularly concentrated over the ~3 Mb gene-rich region, containing SATB1-dependent Rag1 and Rag2 genes.
source: BUR-1 interactions were found particularly concentrated over the ~3 Mb gene-rich region, containing SATB1-dependent Rag1 and Rag2 genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the urea 4C-seq results.

claim: Most of the BUR-1 interactions were absent in SATB1-KO cells, indicating that SATB1 is required for the numerous long-distance interactions over the gene-rich region.
source: In fact, most of the BUR-1 interactions were absent in SATB1-KO cells (Figure 5A, track KO-BUR1), indicating that SATB1 is required for the numerous long-distance interactions over the gene-rich region.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Within the gene-rich region, numerous interactions from SATB1-bound BUR-1 were detected within DNase 1 HS regions containing enhancers marked by H3K27ac and H3Kme1 modifications.
source: Within this gene-rich region, numerous interactions from SATB1-bound BUR-1 were detected within DNase 1 HS regions containing enhancers marked by H3K27ac and H3Kme1 modifications.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the urea 4C-seq results.

claim: BUR-1 interacts with further distal gene-rich region coinciding with enhancer-rich DNase 1 HS regions, where clusters of SATB1 binding sites were detected by standard ChIP-seq, skipping over gene-poor regions and a gene-rich region containing transcriptionally silent olfactory receptor genes.
source: We further examined a wider region covering >44 Mb that includes distal neighboring gene-rich regions (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B). Although interaction frequencies were lower than that within the first ~5.8 Mb gene-rich region, we detected BUR-1 interactions with further distal gene-rich region coinciding with enhancer-rich DNase 1 HS regions, where clusters of SATB1 binding sites were detected by standard ChIP-seq, skipping over gene-poor regions and a gene-rich region containing transcriptionally silent olfactory receptor genes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: Among 49 genes identified with official gene symbols mapped in the 5.8 Mb gene rich region, 3 genes display strong SATB1-dependent expression (adjusted p value<0.05) from RNA-seq data.
source: Concerning the correlation of chromatin interactions and gene expression, among 49 genes identified with official gene symbols mapped in the 5.8 Mb gene rich region, 3 genes display strong SATB1-dependent expression (adjusted p value<0.05) from RNA-seq data (Zelenka et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by RNA-seq data from a cited study.

claim: Rag1 and Rag2 were strongly downregulated and Prrg4 was upregulated upon SATB1 depletion.
source: Rag1 and Rag2 were strongly downregulated and Prrg4 was upregulated upon SATB1 depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the RNA-seq results.

claim: In the two neighboring gene-rich regions that are also engaged in chromatin interactions with BUR-1, expression of 10 additional genes with important roles in thymocytes and T cells were found strongly SATB1 dependent.
source: In the two neighboring gene-rich regions that are also engaged in chromatin interactions with BUR-1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A and B), expression of 10 additional genes with important roles in thymocytes and T cells were found strongly SATB1 dependent. These genes were either up or downregulated upon SATB1 deletion in thymocytes based on RNA-seq data (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is a strong correlation between SATB1-dependent gene expression and extensive looping events over long distances linking SATB1-bound BURs and regulatory regions in the open chromatin regions.
source: Collectively, these data suggest a strong correlation between SATB1-dependent gene expression and extensive looping events over long distances linking SATB1-bound BURs and regulatory regions in the open chromatin regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the urea 4C-seq and RNA-seq data.

claim: SATB1 function on chromatin is not limited to merely connecting a specific target gene locus with nearby enhancers and promoters within TADs.
source: Therefore, SATB1 function on chromatin is not limited to merely connecting a specific target gene locus with nearby enhancers and promoters within TADs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the urea 4C-seq data.

claim: SATB1 appears to form a large interaction network covering the entire gene-rich regions.
source: Instead, SATB1 appears to form a large interaction network covering the entire gene-rich regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the urea 4C-seq data.

claim: BURs were most frequently bound by SATB1 in brain compared to thymocytes, and the least frequently bound in skin.
source: BURs were most frequently bound by SATB1 in brain compared to thymocytes, and the least frequently bound in skin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the cell-type-dependent SATB1 binding.

claim: CTCF binding sites that largely coincide with DNase1 HS were largely similar between the three types of cells (thymocytes, brain, and skin).
source: Whereas SATB1-bound BURs show cell-type dependency, CTCF binding sites that largely coincide with DNase1 HS were largely similar between these three types of cells (Figure 6A, tracks 11-13).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For all three types of cells, high percentages of urea ChIP-seq peaks (close to 80%) correspond to BURs.
source: For all three types of cells, high percentages of urea ChIP-seq peaks (close to 80%, Supplementary file 1) correspond to BURs, as revealed by peak intersection studies using deepTool (Ramírez et al., 2016) and comparing to the BUR reference map (Figure 6C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The number of SATB1-bound BUR peaks greatly differed between cell types despite similar total aligned sequence reads in urea ChIP-seq.
source: Despite similar total aligned sequence reads in urea ChIP-seq, the number of SATB1-bound BUR peaks greatly differed between cell types (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by quantitative analysis.

claim: Among 238,380 mapped BURs (q<0.01), the percentage of SATB1-bound BURs in skin, thymocytes, and brain was 3.7%, 13.5%, and 35.0% (based on average of two replicas/cell type), respectively.
source: Among 238,380 mapped BURs (q<0.01), the percentage of SATB1-bound BURs in skin, thymocytes, and brain was 3.7%, 13.5%, and 35.0% (based on average of two replicas/cell type), respectively (Figure 6D and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Frequency of BURs targeted by SATB1 in vivo can vary more than 10-fold depending on cell type.
source: These results indicate that frequency of BURs targeted by SATB1 in vivo can vary more than 10-fold depending on cell type.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the quantitative analysis.

claim: The majority (83.9%) of BURs targeted by SATB1 in skin were bound to SATB1 in thymocytes.
source: Interestingly, while the number of BURs bound by SATB1 greatly differs between cell types, the majority (83.9%) of BURs targeted by SATB1 in skin were bound to SATB1 in thymocytes, and nearly all (91.6%) SATB1-bound BURs in thymocytes were bound to SATB1 in brain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the overlap of SATB1-bound BURs between cell types.

claim: Nearly all (91.6%) SATB1-bound BURs in thymocytes were bound to SATB1 in brain.
source: Interestingly, while the number of BURs bound by SATB1 greatly differs between cell types, the majority (83.9%) of BURs targeted by SATB1 in skin were bound to SATB1 in thymocytes, and nearly all (91.6%) SATB1-bound BURs in thymocytes were bound to SATB1 in brain.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the overlap of SATB1-bound BURs between cell types.

claim: Each cell type has an overlapping set of SATB1-bound BURs in common, with increasing/decreasing numbers of sites depending on cell type, rather than distinct subsets.
source: Therefore, each cell type has an overlapping set of SATB1-bound BURs in common, with increasing/decreasing numbers of sites depending on cell type, rather than distinct subsets.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the overlap analysis.

claim: The thymus expresses by far the highest levels of SATB1, which comprises ~0.3% of the total protein.
source: In fact, the thymus expresses by far the highest levels of SATB1, which comprises ~0.3% of the total protein (Dickinson and Kohwi-Shigematsu, 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: LADs are large mostly heterochromatic domains in close contact with the nuclear lamina and are known to be enriched in AT-rich sequences.
source: LADs are large mostly heterochromatic domains in close contact with the nuclear lamina and are known to be enriched in AT-rich sequences (Meuleman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by citation to prior study.

claim: The genome-wide distribution of LADs coincides with the majority of SATB1-bound BURs, but it is mutually exclusive with SATB1-bound genomic sites that are mapped by standard ChIP-seq, which avoid LADs.
source: We compared the genomic proximity to lamin B1 (as measured by Dam), SATB1-bound genomic sites (from standard ChIP-seq), SATB1-bound BURs (from urea ChIP-seq) over LADs and flanking regions (±10% outside of the LADs). We found that the genome-wide distribution of LADs coincides with the majority of SATB1-bound BURs, but it is mutually exclusive with SATB1-bound genomic sites that are mapped by standard ChIP-seq, which avoid LADs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CTCF-bound sites mapped by urea-ChIP-seq coincide with those mapped by standard ChIP-seq and are found at LAD borders and inter-LAD regions.
source: In agreement with the result shown in Figure 2A, CTCF-bound sites mapped by urea-ChIP-seq coincide with those mapped by standard ChIP-seq and are found at LAD borders and inter-LAD regions (Figure 7C), as previously described (Guelen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7C and citation to prior study.

claim: At the genome-wide scale, the majority of BURs overlap with LADs.
source: Collectively, these analyses confirmed that the majority of potential BURs from the BUR reference map as well as directly SATB1-bound BURs overlap with LADs (Figure 7B and C), whereas CTCF-binding sites avoid LAD-BUR regions and are confined to inter-LADs and LAD boundaries (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: BURs represent an important sequence component of LADs, some of which are specifically targeted by SATB1.
source: We conclude that, at the genome-wide scale, the majority of BURs overlap with LADs, suggesting that BURs represent an important sequence component of LADs, some of which are specifically targeted by SATB1.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the genome-wide analysis.

claim: The peaks of enhancer histone marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1) corresponded to minimum occupancies of SATB1 in DiPS and also excluded BURs, indicating that enhancers are largely excluded from BURs and SATB1-directly bound BURs in DiPS.
source: We examined the distribution of average signals of SATB1-bound BURs relative to enhancers in DiPS marked by H3K4me1 and H3K27ac modifications over a ±3 kb window centered at H3K4me1 peaks. The peaks of enhancer histone marks (H3K27ac and H3K4me1) corresponded to minimum occupancies of SATB1 in DiPS and also excluded BURs, indicating that enhancers are largely excluded from BURs and SATB1-directly bound BURs in DiPS (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: 18% of SATB1-bound BURs reside in inter-LADs, with 82% found within LADs.
source: We found that 18% of SATB1-bound BURs reside in inter-LADs, with 82% found within LADs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the distribution of SATB1-bound BURs.

claim: Among the SATB1-bound BURs in inter-LADs, 39% or 9.5% of them are located close (within ± 5 kb) to the peaks of H3K4me1 or H3K27ac, respectively.
source: Among the SATB1-bound BURs in inter-LADs, 39% or 9.5% of them are located close (within ± 5 kb) to the peaks of H3K4me1 or H3K27ac, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the proximity of inter-LAD BURs to enhancers.

claim: In inter-LAD regions, as well as in DiPS (locally euchromatic regions within LADs), SATB1-bound BURs generally exclude the peaks of enhancers marked by H3K4me1 and H3K27ac.
source: Importantly, however, genome-wide analyses revealed that in inter-LAD regions, as well as in DiPS (locally euchromatic regions within LADs), SATB1-bound BURs generally exclude the peaks of enhancers marked by H3K4me1 and H3K27ac (Figure 7D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data shown in Figure 7D and E.

claim: SATB1-bound BURs reside in discrete DNase 1-inaccessible chromatin, excluding enhancers and CTCF-bound sites, even in otherwise gene-rich accessible chromatin neighborhoods outside LADs.
source: These results demonstrate that the inter-LAD BURs (BUR-1 and BUR-2), bound to SATB1 nuclear substructure, are contacting accessible chromatin at numerous locations over long distances. Taken together, these data demonstrate that SATB1-bound BURs reside in locally inaccessible chromatin whether they are found inside repressive LADs or in DiPS and in regions within inter-LADs that are otherwise marked as active chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the genome-wide and urea 4C-seq analyses.

claim: The direct binding of SATB1 to BURs within the SATB1-rich nuclear substructure is stable and forms a chromatin scaffold.
source: We propose that the direct binding of SATB1 to BURs within the SATB1-rich nuclear substructure is stable and forms a chromatin scaffold.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed model.

claim: The chromatin scaffold formed by SATB1 binding to BURs interacts dynamically with active gene-rich regions through indirect binding, creating functional chromatin complexes (or hubs) that regulate gene expression depending on the cell type.
source: This chromatin scaffold interacts dynamically with active gene-rich regions through indirect binding, creating functional chromatin complexes (or hubs) that regulate gene expression depending on the cell type.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion as part of the proposed model.
